knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A learned constraint \(L\) is low utility relative to a policy \(\Pi=(W,\phi,A,\theta)\) when the observation window \(W\), event-to-score map \(\phi\), aggregation or aging rule \(A\), and threshold \(\theta\) give \[U_\Pi(L)=A\bigl(\{\phi(e):e\text{ is a recorded use of }L\text{ in }W\}\bigr)\le\theta.\] The classification is observational and policy-relative; it does not imply logical redundancy or absence of future propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Low utility means scoring below a declared policy threshold over a specified observation window; it is not a logical property of the learned constraint.
assumptions_latex: The observation window and recorded event types are fixed.
The scoring, aggregation or aging rule, and threshold are declared.
The learned constraint is logically sound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: U_\Pi(L)\le\theta\Longrightarrow L\text{ is low utility relative to }\Pi,\text{ not necessarily redundant}.
knowledge_statements.title: Policy-Relative Low-Utility Classification

assumptions_latex: Utility is measured over a fixed observation window \(W\) by propagation, conflict participation, or objective-bound improvement.
The learned constraint \(L\) is logically sound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Low observed activity makes \(L\) a deletion candidate, not a logically redundant constraint.

notation.meaning: Observed utility score over window W

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines low utility operationally; it does not equate inactivity with redundancy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a nonnegative score \(U_W(L)\) aggregating uses of \(L\) during \(W\), such as successful propagations, conflict participation, or bound improvements. Relative to threshold \(\theta\), call \(L\) low utility when \(U_W(L)\le\theta\). This classification is observational and policy-dependent: it does not imply that \(L\) is redundant or will never propagate later. Deleting \(L\) preserves correctness when \(L\) is only a learned consequence, but may enlarge future search.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A low-utility learned constraint scores below a chosen activity threshold. This supports deletion heuristics but does not prove redundancy or lack of future usefulness.
knowledge_statements.title: Low-Utility Learned Constraints

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a coherent operational definition and failure boundary, but the utility aggregation, threshold policy, and deletion consequences are solver-dependent and unsupported by any cited empirical or solver-design source.

children.title: Constraint-Quality Indicators
children.top_down_role: Structural indicators used to distinguish promising learned constraints from weak ones.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One convention-explicit LBD-style indicator for learned pseudo-Boolean constraints, not asserted as a universal solver definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a search trail \(\tau\) assigning each currently assigned literal \(\ell\) a decision level \(\operatorname{lev}_\tau(\ell)\). For a learned pseudo-Boolean constraint \(L\) with nonzero-coefficient support \(\operatorname{supp}(L)\), one support-LBD convention is \[\operatorname{LBD}^{\mathrm{supp}}_\tau(L)=\left|\{\operatorname{lev}_\tau(\ell):\ell\in\operatorname{supp}(L),\ \ell\text{ is assigned on }\tau\}\right|.\] It is trail-relative. Conventions counting only falsified, reason-participating, or nonzero-level literals define different indicators and must be named separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under an explicit support-based convention, PB LBD counts distinct trail levels among assigned supported literals; its value depends on both the trail and the declared convention.
assumptions_latex: A search trail and decision-level map are fixed.
The support-based counting convention is explicitly declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{LBD}^{\mathrm{supp}}_\tau(L)\) is not a function of the syntactic constraint \(L\) alone and is not interchangeable with other PB LBD conventions.

notation.meaning: literals having nonzero coefficient in L

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Trail-Relative Support-LBD Convention

assumptions_latex: Each learned constraint \(L\) has nonnegative integer coefficients and a recorded usage history.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Quality indicators rank learned constraints heuristically; no single indicator establishes logical necessity or future utility.

notation.meaning: Number of distinct decision levels represented in L
Number of literals with nonzero coefficient

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates measurable structural and dynamic indicators from logical validity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Structural indicators for \(L\) include its literal count \(|L|\), decision-level diversity \(\operatorname{LBD}(L)\), and coefficient burden \(B(L)=\max_i\lceil\log_2(a_i+1)\rceil\). Dynamic indicators include age, activity, propagation count, and conflict participation. These quantities are computable from \(L\), the trail, and usage counters, but induce only heuristic rankings: equal indicator vectors need not imply equal propagation behavior, and poor scores do not certify redundancy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Size, decision-level diversity, coefficient bit length, age, and activity are measurable quality signals, but they rank constraints heuristically rather than certify usefulness.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Quality Indicators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits an indicators leaf, but no source is cited. In particular, LBD is trail-dependent rather than determined by L alone, and its adaptation to weighted pseudo-Boolean constraints must be tied to a specific definition or solver literature.

children.title: Learned-Database Pressure
children.top_down_role: Storage and search burdens caused by retaining weak learned constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Policy-specific live-size and full-scan bounds under an explicit database representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose each database reduction retains at most \(K\) learned pseudo-Boolean constraints, at most \(q\) constraints are inserted before the next reduction, and each live constraint has at most \(s\) literal occurrences and requires \(O(sB)\) serialized bits including its coefficients, threshold, and amortized metadata. Then between reductions, \[|\mathcal D|\le K+q,\qquad \operatorname{occ}(\mathcal D)\le (K+q)s,\qquad \operatorname{bits}(\mathcal D)=O((K+q)sB).\] An architecture that fully inspects every live occurrence performs \(O((K+q)s)\) occurrence inspections per full scan, excluding coefficient-arithmetic cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A periodic retention cap bounds the live constraint count, literal occurrences, serialized storage, and occurrence inspections of a full scan under the declared representation.
assumptions_latex: \(K,q\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) and \(s,B\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\).
Every reduction finishes before more than \(q\) new constraints are inserted.
Each live constraint obeys the stated occurrence and serialization bounds.
Propagation uses the stated full-scan architecture.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\mathcal D|\le K+q,\quad \operatorname{occ}(\mathcal D)\le(K+q)s,\quad \operatorname{bits}(\mathcal D)=O((K+q)sB).

notation.meaning: Maximum literal occurrences per live constraint
Bit allowance per occurrence in the declared serialization bound

knowledge_statements.title: Periodic Bounded-Retention Envelope

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Retention Cap Does Not Bound Cumulative Learning Work
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of periodic live-database control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A uniform bound \(|\mathcal D_t|\le K+q\) on the live database at each time \(t\) does not bound the total number of constraints generated, scored, inserted, or deleted during a run. For arbitrarily large \(T\), a solver may generate and delete a new constraint in each of \(T\) reduction cycles while respecting the same live-size cap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded live database controls instantaneous storage but not cumulative learning, scoring, insertion, or deletion work.
assumptions_latex: The number of reduction cycles is not independently bounded.
Deleted constraints may be replaced by newly generated constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_t|\mathcal D_t|\le K+q\not\Rightarrow\sum_t|\mathcal G_t|=O(K+q).

notation.meaning: Live learned database at time t

knowledge_statements.title: Retention Cap Does Not Bound Cumulative Learning Work

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Occurrence Caps Do Not Bound Coefficient Storage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of literal-occurrence counts to control explicit PB database size when coefficient bit lengths are unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(N\ge1\), the learned database \(\mathcal D_N=\{2^N x\ge1\}\) contains one constraint and one literal occurrence, but an explicit binary serialization of its coefficient requires \(N+1\) bits. Hence uniform bounds on constraint and literal-occurrence counts do not imply a uniform bit-storage bound without a coefficient-length bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single one-literal PB constraint can require arbitrarily many coefficient bits, so count caps alone do not bound memory.
assumptions_latex: Coefficients are stored explicitly in binary.
The serialization does not replace arbitrary coefficients by fixed-size opaque references.
The database stores the displayed, possibly unnormalized learned constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\mathcal D_N|=\operatorname{occ}(\mathcal D_N)=1\quad\text{while}\quad\operatorname{bits}(\mathcal D_N)=\Omega(N).

notation.meaning: Singleton learned PB database with coefficient \(2^N\).

knowledge_statements.title: Occurrence Caps Do Not Bound Coefficient Storage

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Baseline model-relative cost of a live explicit learned-PB database.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the explicit serialization model, live storage is exactly \(\operatorname{bits}(\mathcal D)\). A propagation pass that fully inspects every stored literal occurrence performs \(\Theta(\operatorname{occ}(\mathcal D))\) occurrence inspections, plus coefficient-arithmetic and indexing costs. Therefore no uniform storage or full-scan bound follows from logical soundness alone when either serialized length or occurrence count is allowed to grow without bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit storage equals serialized database size, and a declared full scan inspects linearly many stored occurrences; soundness alone does not control either quantity.
assumptions_latex: The database uses the declared explicit serialization.
The propagation pass inspects every stored occurrence.
Coefficient-arithmetic and indexing work are accounted for separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_{\mathrm{live}}=\Theta(\operatorname{bits}(\mathcal D)),\qquad I_{\mathrm{fullscan}}=\Theta(\operatorname{occ}(\mathcal D)).

notation.meaning: Bits required for the live explicit database up to fixed serialization overhead.
Number of inspected occurrences in a full scan.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit-Storage and Full-Scan Pressure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation model separating logical records, numeric data, metadata, and propagation indexes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An explicitly serialized learned-PB database is \(\mathcal D=(R,C,Q,M,X)\), where \(R\) stores constraint records and literal identifiers, \(C\) stores signed binary coefficients, \(Q\) stores relation symbols and binary thresholds, \(M\) stores activity, age, scope, and proof-dependency metadata, and \(X\) stores propagation indexes or watch structures. Define \(\operatorname{bits}(\mathcal D)\) as the total serialized length and \(\operatorname{occ}(\mathcal D)\) as the stored literal-occurrence count. Every cost statement must declare whether it includes metadata, indexes, and coefficient arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit learned-PB database separately accounts for records, coefficients, thresholds, metadata, and indexes, with bit size and occurrence count defined by a fixed serialization.
assumptions_latex: Every integer and identifier has a finite explicit encoding.
Shared or compressed objects are counted according to the declared representation.
The serialization convention is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{bits}(\mathcal D)=|R|_{\mathrm{bit}}+|C|_{\mathrm{bit}}+|Q|_{\mathrm{bit}}+|M|_{\mathrm{bit}}+|X|_{\mathrm{bit}}.
knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Learned-PB Database Serialization Model

assumptions_latex: A learned database \(\mathcal D\) stores pseudo-Boolean constraints explicitly.
Propagation scans or indexes stored literals and performs coefficient arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without deletion or compaction, accumulated learned constraints can make memory and propagation costs dominate search.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States storage and scan bounds for explicit learned pseudo-Boolean databases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an explicit database \(\mathcal D\), storing coefficients in binary requires \(\Omega\!\left(\sum_{L\in\mathcal D}|L|\right)\) words and \(O\!\left(\sum_{L\in\mathcal D}|L|B(L)\right)\) bits, excluding indexing overhead. A full propagation scan costs at least linear time in the inspected literal occurrences, plus coefficient-arithmetic cost. Thus unbounded growth of \(\mathcal D\) yields unbounded memory and scan pressure even when every learned constraint is sound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit learned constraints consume storage proportional to their literals and coefficient sizes; unchecked database growth also increases propagation and maintenance work.
knowledge_statements.title: Learned-Database Pressure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record is placed in a failure-regime taxonomy but is labeled complexity_bound. Its word lower bound also depends on the machine word model and coefficient representation, while the scan claim depends on propagation architecture. An authoritative implementation or complexity source and a corrected role, likely failure_boundary, are required.

children.title: Uncertified Preprocessing Transformations
children.top_down_role: Instance reductions lacking proof support for their semantic effects.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes semantic validity of preprocessing from evidence accepted by an end-to-end checker.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a checker \(V\), a proof format \(\mathcal F\), and an original-instance claim \(Q\), a transformation from \(P\) to \(P'\) is certified for \(Q\) when \(V\) accepts an \(\mathcal F\)-record establishing every transformation relation needed to derive \(Q(P)\) from the certified claim about \(P'\). If no accepted record or independently checked original-instance evidence supplies a required relation, a certificate for \(P'\) alone does not certify \(Q(P)\). This is an evidence failure even when the transformation is semantically valid; conversely, omitted transformation evidence is immaterial when \(Q(P)\) is checked independently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Preprocessing certification is relative to a checker, proof format, and lifted claim. Solving the reduced instance is insufficient when a required transformation relation is unchecked, although independent checking of the original claim can make the omitted transformation record irrelevant.
assumptions_latex: A declared checker \(V\) and proof format \(\mathcal F\) determine accepted evidence.
The original-instance claim \(Q\) determines which feasibility, solution, or objective relations are required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{A required relation is neither accepted nor independently established}\Rightarrow\text{the reduced-instance certificate does not certify }Q(P).
knowledge_statements.title: Checker-Relative Preprocessing Certification Boundary

assumptions_latex: A preprocessor maps an original optimization instance \(P\) to a reduced instance \(P'\).
Correctness requires a stated relation between feasible solutions and objective values of \(P\) and \(P'\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without a checkable witness for the transformation relation, correctness of the preprocessing step is outside end-to-end certification.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concerns missing evidence, not whether the preprocessing transformation is actually incorrect.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A preprocessing transformation is certified only if a checker can validate from \(T\) the claimed relation between \(P\) and \(P'\), including feasibility preservation and any objective correspondence needed by the optimization claim. If the solver emits \(P'\) without such a checkable \(T\), then a certificate for solving \(P'\) alone does not certify the corresponding claim for \(P\). The transformation is uncertified even when it is semantically correct.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solving a reduced instance does not certify the original instance unless a checker can validate how preprocessing preserved feasibility and objective claims.
knowledge_statements.title: Uncertified Preprocessing Transformations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary role and distinction between semantic correctness and certification are appropriate, but no certified-preprocessing or proof-logging source is cited. The required feasibility and objective correspondence also depends on the stated certificate system and claim type.

children.title: Uncertified Assignment Reconstruction
children.top_down_role: Recovered assignments lacking checkable links to the preprocessed instance.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evidence needed to certify a reported original assignment from a reduced assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y\in\operatorname{Feas}(P')\) and let \(x\) be a reported assignment for the original instance \(P\). Assignment reconstruction is certified when the checker either verifies \(x\in\operatorname{Feas}(P)\) directly or accepts a reconstruction witness establishing that \((y,x)\) satisfies the declared extension relation \(E\), where \(E\) entails \(x\in\operatorname{Feas}(P)\). Reduced feasibility alone certifies neither a particular reported \(x\) nor the existence of an extension unless that implication is itself checked. A missing reconstruction log is harmless when direct checking of \(x\) supplies the required original-feasibility evidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible reduced assignment does not by itself certify a reported original assignment. Certification requires either direct checking of that assignment or a checked extension witness; therefore an omitted reconstruction log is not a gap when direct original-feasibility checking is available.
assumptions_latex: \(y\) is a checked feasible assignment for the reduced instance \(P'\).
The claim concerns a particular original assignment \(x\), or the existence of an original feasible extension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y\in\operatorname{Feas}(P')\not\Rightarrow x\in\operatorname{Feas}(P)\text{ without a checked direct-feasibility or extension implication}.

notation.meaning: declared extension relation linking reduced and original assignments

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment-Reconstruction Evidence Boundary

assumptions_latex: A reduced-instance assignment \(y\) satisfies the preprocessed constraints of \(P'\).
A reconstruction map is intended to produce an original-variable assignment \(x=R(y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Absent a checkable reconstruction witness, feasibility of \(y\) does not certify feasibility of the claimed original assignment \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Targets eliminated variables and other assignment reconstruction omitted from the certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assignment reconstruction is certified when a checker can compute or validate \(x=R(y)\) and verify \(x\in\operatorname{Feas}(P)\) from the logged preprocessing data. If eliminated-variable values, substitutions, or extension conditions are omitted, then \(y\in\operatorname{Feas}(P')\) alone establishes neither that \(R(y)\) is defined nor that the reported \(x\) satisfies \(P\). This is an evidence gap independent of whether the internal reconstruction algorithm is correct.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible reduced assignment does not certify an original assignment when eliminated-variable reconstruction and its feasibility checks are absent from the evidence.
knowledge_statements.title: Uncertified Assignment Reconstruction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record matches the assignment-reconstruction evidence-gap leaf, but it has no source. A certified reconstruction reference is needed to support the requirements imposed on R, eliminated-variable data, and checker validation.

children.title: Uncertified Objective Reconstruction
children.top_down_role: Recovered objective values lacking checkable preservation evidence.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evidence required to lift reduced objective values, bounds, or optima to the original objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) and \(y\) be corresponding original and reduced solutions with objectives \(f(x)\) and \(g(y)\). Objective reconstruction is certified only when the checker validates a relation strong enough for the claim being lifted. Exact value recovery requires a checked value relation, such as \(f(x)=\phi(g(y))\). For minimization, a checked positive-affine relation \(f(x)=a g(y)+b\), \(a>0\), translates reduced bounds and optima by \(z\mapsto az+b\) and preserves ordering. Without an applicable checked relation—including every offset, scale, substitution, and eliminated contribution—a reduced value, bound, or optimum does not certify its asserted original-objective counterpart. Direct recomputation of \(f(x)\) can independently certify the value of a reported reconstructed assignment, but not translation of a global reduced bound unless the global correspondence is checked.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective evidence must match the claim: exact values need a checked value relation, and reduced global bounds or optima need a checked global correspondence. Directly recomputing a reported assignment's original cost does not by itself translate a reduced global bound.
assumptions_latex: The optimization direction and the original and reduced objective semantics are fixed.
The correspondence is asserted only over the solution pairs and feasible sets relevant to the lifted claim.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{No applicable checked objective relation}\Rightarrow\text{no certified translation of the asserted reduced value, bound, or optimum}.

notation.meaning: positive scale and additive offset in an affine translation

knowledge_statements.title: Claim-Aware Objective-Reconstruction Boundary

assumptions_latex: The original and reduced objectives are \(f(x)\) and \(g(y)\), respectively.
Preprocessing may introduce an offset, scaling, substitution, or eliminated objective term.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A bound or optimum for \(g\) does not certify the corresponding value for \(f\) without a checkable objective relation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes offsets, scaling, substitutions, and eliminated objective contributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Objective reconstruction is certified only when the evidence validates a relation such as \(f(R(y))=\phi(g(y))\) for every relevant reduced solution \(y\), with \(\phi\) explicitly accounting for offsets, scaling, and eliminated terms. Without this relation, a certified reduced bound \(g(y)\ge\beta\) or reduced optimum \(g^*\) cannot be translated into a certified bound or optimum for \(f\). Feasibility reconstruction alone is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduced objective values certify original values only when logged evidence validates every offset, scaling factor, substitution, and eliminated contribution.
knowledge_statements.title: Uncertified Objective Reconstruction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure boundary is locally appropriate, but no optimization-certificate source is supplied. The example bound g(y) greater than or equal to beta presupposes an optimization direction, and the equality through phi may be stronger than the correspondence needed by some preprocessing rules; both must be grounded in a specified certificate framework.

children.title: Transformation-Trace Gaps
children.top_down_role: Missing records that prevent end-to-end checking across preprocessing stages.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Claim-relative completeness of a multi-stage preprocessing and reconstruction trace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_0,\ldots,P_k\) be instances connected by claimed relations \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\). A trace is complete for an end-to-end claim \(Q\) when the checker accepts evidence for every relation required by a valid composition deriving \(Q(P_0)\) from the checked claim about \(P_k\), including required assignment and objective maps. If a required relation is neither checked nor derivable from other accepted records, the trace does not certify \(Q(P_0)\). A missing redundant or claim-irrelevant record does not by itself create this gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An end-to-end preprocessing trace is incomplete exactly when a relation needed to lift the checked final-instance claim to the original instance is neither checked nor otherwise derivable; irrelevant or redundant omissions do not break certification.
assumptions_latex: \(P_0,\ldots,P_k\) are the successive instances in the declared transformation chain.
The certificate system specifies which accepted relations compose to establish the original-instance claim \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl(\exists j:\ C_j\text{ is required for }Q\text{ and is neither checked nor derivable}\bigr)\Rightarrow Q(P_0)\text{ is not certified by the trace}.
knowledge_statements.title: Required-Link Transformation-Trace Gap

assumptions_latex: Preprocessing applies transformations \(T_1,\ldots,T_k\) to obtain \(P_k\) from \(P_0\).
The final claim depends on composing their feasibility or objective correspondences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If any required transformation record is missing or uncheckable, the composed certificate chain from \(P_k\) to \(P_0\) is incomplete.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes completeness of a multi-step preprocessing and reconstruction trace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A complete transformation trace supplies, for every \(j=1,\ldots,k\), checkable data establishing the required relation between \(P_{j-1}\) and \(P_j\), together with sufficient information to compose assignment and objective maps. If some \(T_j\) is absent, ambiguous, or accepted only by an unverified implementation, the checker cannot derive the end-to-end relation between \(P_0\) and \(P_k\). Certificates downstream of the gap certify at most the suffix beginning after it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A preprocessing certificate is only as complete as its transformation chain; one missing or uncheckable step breaks end-to-end reconstruction and objective certification.
knowledge_statements.title: Transformation-Trace Gaps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind fits the trace-gap leaf, but no certified-preprocessing source supports the completeness conditions or the assertion that downstream certificates certify at most a suffix. Those claims depend on the proof system's composition and recovery rules.

children.title: Unsupported Hybrid Reasoning
children.top_down_role: Mixed reasoning components whose inferences lack a common checkable representation.

assumptions_latex: A hybrid solver combines pseudo-Boolean inference with another reasoning engine \(E\), such as linear programming.
A final certificate contains conclusions derived using both components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any hybrid inference lacking a checkable derivation in the accepted proof system remains outside the certified conclusion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to cross-engine inferences not translated into the checker's accepted proof rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose engine \(E\) produces a constraint, bound, or infeasibility claim \(C_E\) used by subsequent pseudo-Boolean reasoning. End-to-end certification requires either a derivation of \(C_E\) in \(\mathcal P\) or independently checkable evidence whose acceptance rule is part of \(\mathcal P\). If neither is supplied, later steps depending on \(C_E\) may be internally valid yet do not yield a \(\mathcal P\)-certificate of the final claim. Trusting \(E\)'s output enlarges the trusted computing base.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hybrid reasoning is uncertified when conclusions imported from another engine lack a derivation or independently checkable witness accepted by the proof checker.
knowledge_statements.title: Unsupported Hybrid Reasoning

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly targets unsupported cross-engine evidence and failure_boundary is the right role, but no hybrid proof-logging source is cited. The conclusion depends on a formally specified proof system, accepted evidence rules, and trusted computing base.

children.title: Unsupported LP Reasoning
children.top_down_role: Linear-programming deductions or bounds not represented in the proof artifact.

knowledge_statements.title: Unsupported LP Reasoning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for accepting LP-derived claims in a Boolean-optimization certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a Boolean optimization instance, \(R(F)\) an LP relaxation, and \(C\) a certificate checked by verifier \(V\). An LP-derived assertion \(a\) in \(C\) is supported only if \(V\) checks either a direct derivation of \(a\) from the encoded constraints of \(R(F)\), or a sound independently checkable LP witness for \(a\). If neither check occurs, then acceptance of \(C\) depends on an unverified LP-solver result. Consequently, \(V(C,F)=\mathrm{accept}\) does not by itself certify any conclusion whose derivation requires \(a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An LP-based assertion cannot support a certified Boolean-optimization conclusion unless the verifier checks its derivation or a sound LP witness.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) checks only explicitly specified certificate rules.
\(a\) is necessary for the claimed conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\neg\operatorname{Checked}_V(a)\Rightarrow \neg\operatorname{Certified}_V(\operatorname{claim}(C))\).

children.title: Cross-Engine Evidence Gaps
children.top_down_role: Missing justification at interfaces between SAT, PB, LP, or optimization engines.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Engine Evidence Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compositional boundary for certificates produced by multiple reasoning engines.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let engines \(E_1,\ldots,E_k\) produce evidence objects \(c_1,\ldots,c_k\), and let \(D\) be the directed dependency graph restricted to evidence relevant to the final claim, where an edge \(c_i\to c_j\) means that checking \(c_j\) uses a conclusion exported by \(E_i\). A composite verifier certifies the final claim only if every evidence object in \(D\) is checked and every cross-engine edge in \(D\) is validated by a sound translation rule preserving the asserted semantics. If an edge in \(D\) lacks such a checked rule, separately valid component certificates do not imply validity of the composite claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Individually checked engine outputs do not certify a composite result when a relevant dependency crosses engines without a checked, semantics-preserving translation.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) contains exactly the evidence dependencies relevant to the final claim.
Each local checker is sound for its declared semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists(c_i\to c_j)\in D\;\neg\operatorname{CheckedBridge}(c_i,c_j)\Rightarrow\neg\operatorname{Certified}(\operatorname{final})\).

dependency graph restricted to evidence relevant to the final claim

children.title: Trusted-Component Expansion
children.top_down_role: Growth of the unverified computing base caused by unsupported reasoning components.

knowledge_statements.title: Trusted-Component Expansion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of enlarging the trusted computing base of a certificate checker.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a claimed result \(q\), let \(T\) be the trusted component set and \(U\) the evidence checked independently of \(T\). If an unchecked engine \(E\) is added to obtain \(T'=T\cup\{E\}\), then conclusions emitted by \(E\) may be accepted without certificates, but soundness becomes conditional on \(E\)'s correctness. Thus the independently certified guarantee weakens from correctness conditional on every component in \(T\) to correctness conditional on every component in \(T'\). Moving a component into the trusted base removes an evidence gap only by adding a trust assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Declaring an unchecked engine trusted closes its evidence gap only by enlarging the assumptions on which the certified result depends.
assumptions_latex: \(E\notin T\) initially.
No independently checked certificate establishes every conclusion exported by \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Sound}(q\mid T')\) requires \(\operatorname{Correct}(E)\) in addition to the assumptions required by \(\operatorname{Sound}(q\mid T)\).
review_flags: trusted-computing-base principle is unambiguous but unsupported by supplied locators

children.title: Proof-Size Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Certificate growth that stresses storage, transfer, or generation resources.

knowledge_statements.title: Proof-Size Bottlenecks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate length as a necessary verification resource.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\pi(x)\) be an explicitly encoded certificate for instance \(x\), with bit length \(|\pi(x)|\), and let a verifier read the certificate through a sequential input interface. Any verifier whose acceptance can depend on every certificate bit has worst-case checking time \(\Omega(|\pi(x)|)\). Hence, for a family \(\{x_n\}\), certificates satisfying \(|\pi(x_n)|\ge g(n)\) impose an input-processing bottleneck of \(\Omega(g(n))\), regardless of the cost of individual inference checks. Superpolynomially large mandatory certificates therefore preclude polynomial total verification time in this model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit certificates require time at least proportional to their length; necessarily huge proofs therefore bottleneck verification before inference checking is considered.
assumptions_latex: Certificates are explicitly encoded and read sequentially.
Acceptance may depend on every encoded certificate bit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_V(x,\pi)=\Omega(|\pi|)\), and \(|\pi(x_n)|\ge g(n)\Rightarrow T_V(x_n,\pi(x_n))=\Omega(g(n))\).

children.title: Proof-Checking Time Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Verification workloads dominated by lengthy certificate processing.

knowledge_statements.title: Proof-Checking Time Bottlenecks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregate time required to check certificate inference steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a certificate \(\pi=(s_1,\ldots,s_m)\) contain \(m\) inference steps, and let \(t_i\) be the time required to parse and validate step \(s_i\), including access to its premises. A verifier that checks every step has total checking time \(T_V(\pi)\ge\sum_{i=1}^{m}t_i\). If \(t_i\ge c>0\) for all \(i\), then \(T_V(\pi)=\Omega(m)\); if some step requires solving an auxiliary problem of cost \(h(n)\), then \(T_V(\pi)=\Omega(h(n))\). Either many steps or expensive local checks can therefore dominate certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Checking time is at least the aggregate cost of validated steps, so numerous inferences or one expensive auxiliary check can become the bottleneck.
assumptions_latex: Every inference step must be validated before acceptance.
\(t_i\) includes parsing, premise access, and the declared local check.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_V(\pi)\ge\sum_{i=1}^{m}t_i\), hence \(T_V(\pi)=\Omega(m)\) when \(\inf_i t_i>0\).

source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

children.title: Proof-Checking Memory Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Verification workloads exceeding practical memory capacity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Peak verifier working space under explicit retention, excluding read-only certificate storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a topological checking order for a certificate dependency DAG \(D_\pi\). At time \(t\), let \(\operatorname{Live}_t\) contain previously derived objects that must remain explicitly available for an unprocessed check, and let object \(u\) occupy \(b(u)\) bits. For a verifier required to retain those objects without recomputation, auxiliary working memory satisfies \(M_V(\pi)\ge\max_t\sum_{u\in\operatorname{Live}_t}b(u)\). If every live object occupies at least \(b\) bits and \(L=\max_t|\operatorname{Live}_t|\), then \(M_V(\pi)\ge bL\). The bound is order- and model-relative: deletion after last use can reduce liveness, while deleting earlier requires rereading or recomputation and can trade space for time. Certificate input storage is a separate resource unless the machine model requires it to reside in working memory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Peak checker working memory is at least the total size of simultaneously live derived objects under an explicit-retention model. The bound depends on checking order and reclamation; recomputation can trade time for space, and certificate storage is distinct from auxiliary memory.
assumptions_latex: \(D_\pi\) is acyclic and the checker uses a fixed topological order.
Every object in \(\operatorname{Live}_t\) must be explicitly retained and is not recomputed while live.
\(M_V\) measures auxiliary working memory separately from read-only certificate input unless stated otherwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M_V(\pi)\ge\max_t\sum_{u\in\operatorname{Live}_t}b(u)\ge bL.

notation.meaning: derived objects retained at time t for future checks
encoded working-space footprint of object u

knowledge_statements.title: Live-Dependency Working-Space Bound
Proof-Checking Memory Bottlenecks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Peak working memory required by certificate dependency structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_\pi\) be the acyclic dependency graph of a certificate \(\pi\). During a fixed topological checking order, call a previously derived object live when it has an unprocessed successor. If live objects must be retained explicitly and each requires at least \(b\) bits, then the verifier's peak working memory is at least \(bL\), where \(L\) is the maximum number of simultaneously live objects. Thus certificate size alone does not determine memory: wide or long-lived dependency frontiers can force \(M_V(\pi)=\Omega(bL)\), even when individual inference rules use constant auxiliary space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Verification memory is governed by the largest live dependency frontier; many simultaneously needed derived objects can exhaust memory despite cheap local rules.
assumptions_latex: The verifier follows a fixed topological order of \(D_\pi\).
Live derived objects are retained explicitly and occupy at least \(b\) bits each.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_V(\pi)\ge bL\), where \(L=\max_t|\operatorname{Live}_t(D_\pi)|\).

children.title: Certificate Granularity Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Size, detail, and checker-effort implications of certificate granularity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract accounting relation between certificate block size, repeated overhead, and validation work.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition \(N\) elementary inferences into \(k\) nonempty blocks of sizes \(g_1,\ldots,g_k\), with \(\sum_{j=1}^k g_j=N\). If each block contributes \(a\ge0\) bits of fixed overhead, its total fixed overhead is \(ak\). If validating block \(j\) costs \(q_j(g_j)\), total block-validation work is \(\sum_{j=1}^k q_j(g_j)\). Merging blocks weakly reduces fixed overhead because it reduces \(k\), but it reduces checking work only when the validation cost of each merged block does not exceed the sum of the costs of the blocks it replaces. Thus coarser granularity need not improve checking time and may alter peak working memory or the locality of independently checkable steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coarser certificate blocks reduce repeated per-block overhead, but reduce checking time only when merged blocks are no more expensive to validate than their components. Granularity can also change memory use and local auditability.
assumptions_latex: The certificate is partitioned into nonempty blocks covering all \(N\) elementary inferences.
Fixed overhead and block-validation cost are measured under one declared encoding and checker model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_{\mathrm{fixed}}=ak,\qquad T_{\mathrm{blocks}}=\sum_{j=1}^k q_j(g_j),
knowledge_statements.title: Block-Granularity Cost Tradeoff
Certificate Granularity Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tradeoff between inference aggregation and local checking cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a derivation with \(N\) elementary inferences is partitioned into certificate blocks of size \(g\), where \(1\le g\le N\). If each block carries overhead \(a>0\) and validating a block of size \(g\) costs \(q(g)\), then, ignoring rounding, certificate overhead is \(aN/g\) and checking work is \((N/g)q(g)\). Increasing \(g\) reduces block count and overhead, but it improves checking time only when \(q(g)/g\) does not increase. Coarse blocks may therefore shorten a certificate while making each step harder or less independently auditable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Larger certificate steps reduce repeated encoding overhead, but can increase local validation cost and reduce auditability; the best granularity depends on per-block checking cost.
assumptions_latex: \(N\) elementary inferences are grouped into blocks of uniform size \(g\).
Each block has encoding overhead \(a\) and validation cost \(q(g)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_{\mathrm{over}}(g)=aN/g\) and \(T_{\mathrm{check}}(g)=(N/g)q(g)\).
review_flags: tradeoff is derived under an explicit abstract cost model

children.title: Objective-Semantics Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Unclear interpretation of weights, priorities, offsets, or reported optimum values.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Semantics Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambiguity in the optimization objective interpreted by a verifier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the same feasible set \(X\) be paired with two admissible objective interpretations \(f_1,f_2:X\to\mathbb{Q}\), including their optimization directions and numerical conventions. The objective semantics are ambiguous when the instance encoding and verifier specification do not select one interpretation and there exists \(x\in X\) with \(f_1(x)\ne f_2(x)\), or the selected optima differ. In that case, a certificate asserting an objective value \(z\) cannot establish an unqualified optimization claim, because \(z\) may denote different values or bounds under the two admissible interpretations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A value certificate is inconclusive when the model and verifier permit distinct objective functions, directions, or numerical conventions that yield different meanings.
assumptions_latex: \(X\ne\varnothing\).
Both \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) are consistent with the available objective specification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Ambiguous}(f_1,f_2)\Rightarrow\neg\operatorname{Certified}(\text{unqualified objective claim})\).
review_flags: objective locator is provisional; ambiguity-to-certification boundary needs direct support

children.title: Certificate-Semantics Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Unclear meaning of proof records, bounds, or witness artifacts.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate-Semantics Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambiguity in what a submitted certificate is claimed to establish.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A(F,C)\) mean that certificate \(C\) for instance \(F\) is accepted by a syntactic checker, and let \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) be distinct semantic predicates compatible with the certificate specification, such as feasibility, a bound, or global optimality. Certificate semantics are ambiguous when the specification does not select one predicate and there exists an accepted pair \((F,C)\) for which \(P_1(F,C)\ne P_2(F,C)\). In that case, syntactic acceptance alone does not determine which semantic predicate the certificate is intended to establish and therefore cannot certify an unqualified semantic claim without an additional interpretation rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certificate acceptance does not determine an unqualified semantic claim when the specification permits distinct interpretations that disagree on an accepted certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(P_1\ne P_2\) are both compatible with the certificate specification.
\(A(F,C)\) records only syntactic acceptance absent an interpretation rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl[\exists(F,C):A(F,C)\land P_1(F,C)\ne P_2(F,C)\bigr]\Rightarrow\neg\operatorname{UniqueSemantics}(A)\).

children.title: Objective–Certificate Value Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Disagreement between certified values and the objective interpretation of the instance.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective–Certificate Value Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency boundary between modeled and certificate-reported objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in X\) be the solution encoded by certificate \(C\), let \(f:X\to\mathbb{Q}\) be the declared objective, and let \(z_C\) be the value asserted by \(C\). Under a fixed common scaling, sign, offset, and rounding convention, objective-value consistency requires \(z_C=f(x)\). If \(z_C\ne f(x)\), then \(C\) cannot certify the claimed value or an optimality statement using that value, even when \(x\) is feasible. A verifier must recompute \(f(x)\) exactly or validate a sound arithmetic derivation connecting \(x\) to \(z_C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible solution does not certify the reported objective or optimality when its recomputed objective differs from the certificate value under the declared conventions.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in X\) is the certificate-encoded solution.
Objective scaling, sign, offset, and rounding conventions are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(z_C
e f(x)\Rightarrow
eg\operatorname{Certified}(z_C)\land
eg\operatorname{Certified}(\operatorname{optimality\ based\ on\ }z_C)\).

children.title: Optimization-Claim Coverage Gaps
children.top_down_role: Certificates that support feasibility or bounds without covering the full optimization claim.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimization-Claim Coverage Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between feasibility evidence and a complete optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization of \(f\) over \(X\), a complete exact optimality certificate for value \(z\) must establish both an upper bound and a matching lower bound: there exists \(x\in X\) with \(f(x)\le z\), and every \(y\in X\) satisfies \(f(y)\ge z\). Evidence establishing only feasibility, only one bound, or only exclusion of some improving solutions leaves a coverage gap. Without both implications, the evidence does not entail \(\min_{y\in X}f(y)=z\). The inequalities reverse analogously for maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact optimality requires matching primal and global bound evidence; feasibility or a one-sided bound alone leaves the optimization claim uncertified.
assumptions_latex: \(X\ne\varnothing\).
The claimed task is exact minimization with finite reported value \(z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl[\exists x\in X:f(x)\le z\bigr]\land\bigl[\forall y\in X:f(y)\ge z\bigr]\Rightarrow\min_{y\in X}f(y)=z\); omission of either conjunct does not establish this equality.
review_flags: locator is provisional and may not explicitly formulate certificate coverage

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coverage required for an exact infeasibility claim in finite Boolean optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a Boolean feasible set \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\), an exact infeasibility claim requires checked evidence entailing \(X=\varnothing\). Failure to find an incumbent, refutation of one assignment, or certified infeasibility of only a proper subregion \(R\subsetneq\{0,1\}^n\) does not establish global infeasibility unless checked regions collectively cover the entire candidate domain. Thus local exclusion evidence with uncovered residual assignments leaves the infeasibility claim uncertified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global infeasibility requires checked exclusion of every candidate assignment; failure to find a solution or refuting only part of the Boolean domain leaves a coverage gap.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) is the feasible set of the declared finite Boolean instance.
Each regional refutation is sound for its declared region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcup_{i=1}^m R_i=\{0,1\}^n\land\forall i\;(X\cap R_i=\varnothing)\Rightarrow X=\varnothing\); if \(\{0,1\}^n\setminus\bigcup_iR_i\ne\varnothing\), the regional refutations alone do not entail \(X=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: feasible set of the Boolean optimization instance
candidate-domain region covered by a checked infeasibility certificate

children.title: SAT Foundations Boundary
children.top_down_role: Foundational satisfiability material treated as prerequisite knowledge.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical complexity and witness boundary for explicitly encoded CNF satisfiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: CNF-SAT is NP-complete. If a CNF formula F is satisfiable, a total assignment is a certificate verifiable in time polynomial in |F|. In any sound proof system with polynomial-time proof checking, an unsatisfiability refutation is checkable in time polynomial in its encoded length, but such refutations need not have polynomial length in |F| for a fixed proof system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: CNF-SAT is NP-complete; satisfying assignments are short witnesses, while checkable refutations of unsatisfiability need not be short.
assumptions_latex: F is an explicitly encoded finite CNF formula.
The refutation statement concerns a fixed sound proof system with polynomial-time proof checking.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{CNF\text{-}SAT}\text{ is NP-complete, and }F(x)=1\text{ is verifiable in time polynomial in }|F|.
knowledge_statements.title: SAT Decision and Certificate Boundary
SAT Foundations Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates propositional satisfiability foundations from optimization-specific reasoning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a propositional formula \(F\), the SAT task asks whether there exists an assignment \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) such that \(F(x)=1\); an assignment certifies satisfiability, while an appropriate refutation certifies unsatisfiability. These foundations do not by themselves define an objective function, compare feasible assignments, or certify an optimal value. A Boolean optimization problem \(\min\{f(x):F(x)=1\}\) therefore lies beyond the SAT-foundation boundary whenever its claim depends on \(f\), objective bounds, or exclusion of all better feasible assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SAT foundations certify existence or nonexistence of satisfying assignments, but optimization additionally requires objective semantics and evidence excluding better solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a propositional formula over \(n\) Boolean variables.
\(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb{Q}\) is external to the SAT decision predicate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{SAT}(F)\) alone does not entail \(\min\{f(x):F(x)=1\}=z\) for any specified \(z\).
review_flags: standard SAT-versus-optimization boundary lacks a relevant supplied source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The SAT-versus-optimization boundary is mathematically standard and fits the terminal container, but no authoritative SAT or proof-system source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: CDCL Foundations Boundary
children.top_down_role: Core conflict-driven search material treated as prerequisite knowledge.

knowledge_statements.title: CDCL Foundations Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates propositional CDCL decision machinery from optimization-specific mechanisms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a CNF formula \(F=\bigwedge_{j=1}^m C_j\) over finitely many Boolean variables, foundational CDCL maintains a partial assignment, applies unit propagation, selects decision literals, analyzes conflicts, and learns only clauses \(C\) satisfying \(F\models C\). Exhaustive search with sound learning can return a satisfying assignment or certify that \(F\) is unsatisfiable. If an objective \(f\) is attached to satisfying assignments, these operations alone neither maintain an incumbent nor certify that no assignment has objective value below a candidate bound. Thus foundational CDCL is a feasibility-and-refutation framework, not by itself an optimization algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: CDCL decides CNF satisfiability through propagation, decisions, conflicts, and implied learned clauses; without objective bounds or an optimization loop, it does not certify optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF formula.
Every learned clause \(C\) satisfies \(F\models C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Foundational CDCL certifies \(F\in\{\mathrm{SAT},\mathrm{UNSAT}\}\), but does not alone certify \(x^\star\in\arg\min\{f(x):x\models F\}\).
review_flags: No supplied source locator covers the precise CDCL soundness and optimization boundary.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and mathematical distinction are appropriate, but no citation supports the stated CDCL soundness, completeness, and optimization limitation.

children.title: Optimization-Specific CDCL Extensions
children.top_down_role: CDCL adaptations included only where they directly support MaxSAT or PB optimization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact CDCL optimization by repeated feasibility tests under progressively stronger objective bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:x\models F\} and let f:X\to\mathbb Z. After finding x^k\in X with U_k=f(x^k), add an exact encoding of f(x)\le U_k-1. If the strengthened formula is satisfiable, update the incumbent; if it is unsatisfiable, x^k is globally optimal. Linear descent tests successive bounds, whereas binary threshold search tests intermediate bounds in a known finite objective interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated SAT solving below the incumbent is exact: a model improves the incumbent, while refutation of the strict-improvement bound proves optimality.
assumptions_latex: X is finite.
f is integer-valued and every objective-bound encoding is exact.
Every reported satisfiability or unsatisfiability result is sound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\land(f\le U_k-1)\text{ is unsatisfiable}\Longrightarrow \min_{x\in X}f(x)=U_k.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Objective-Bound Search

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-query complexity excluding the cost of individual CDCL calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every feasible objective value is integral and lies in [L,U], and a feasible threshold is known. Sequential threshold descent requires at most U-L+1 feasibility queries, including a possible final infeasible strict-improvement query. Binary search for the least feasible integer threshold requires at most \lceil\log_2(U-L+1)\rceil threshold queries when an endpoint invariant identifies one feasible endpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential descent uses linearly many threshold queries, while binary threshold search uses logarithmically many; these bounds do not bound the cost of each SAT call.
assumptions_latex: L,U\in\mathbb Z are valid objective bounds.
Threshold feasibility is monotone and encoded exactly.
The query count excludes construction and solving time within each query.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q_{\mathrm{linear}}\le U-L+1,\qquad Q_{\mathrm{binary}}\le\lceil\log_2(U-L+1)\rceil.
review_flags: The binary bound presupposes the stated endpoint invariant; alternative initialization conventions can add a constant number of queries.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Threshold Query Bounds
Optimization-Specific CDCL Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the additional invariant needed to turn CDCL feasibility search into exact Boolean optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:x\models F\}\) and let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\). A CDCL-based method is an exact minimization method only if it adds an optimization mechanism that maintains an incumbent value \(U\), excludes or refutes every region capable of containing a point with value below \(U\), and terminates only after establishing \(f(x)\ge U\) for all \(x\in X\). Such mechanisms include objective-bound constraints, linear or binary bound search, and core-guided relaxation. Conflict learning remains sound search support, but optimality follows from the global bound or exhaustion certificate rather than from clause learning alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimization-specific CDCL must combine learned-clause search with incumbent management and a global lower-bound or exhaustion certificate; clause learning alone proves no objective optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite and each objective comparison used by the method is exact.
All added clauses and bound constraints preserve the assignments not yet excluded by the optimization argument.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Termination is valid only with \(x^\star\in X\) and \(f(x)\ge f(x^\star)\) for every \(x\in X\).
review_flags: No supplied locator supports a specific optimization-CDCL framework or its termination certificate.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record fits the optimization-extension boundary, but the asserted incumbent, exclusion, and termination requirements and the listed CDCL optimization mechanisms lack a source locator.

children.title: Polyhedral Optimization Boundary
children.top_down_role: General polyhedral theory beyond the Boolean optimization interfaces used here.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Optimization Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes exact Boolean optimization from optimization over a continuous polyhedral relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty finite set \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), linear optimization over the exact polytope \(P=\operatorname{conv}(X)\) satisfies \(\min\{c^\top x:x\in P\}=\min\{c^\top x:x\in X\}\). If a formulation instead uses a polyhedron \(Q\supsetneq P\), its optimum is only a lower bound for minimization and may be attained at a fractional point. Consequently, a polyhedral interface is exact only when its formulation describes \(P\), or when additional branching, cutting, or integrality enforcement closes the relaxation gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimizing over the convex hull of feasible Boolean points is exact; optimizing over a larger polyhedral relaxation may yield only a fractional lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) is nonempty and finite.
\(P=\operatorname{conv}(X)\) and \(Q\) is a polyhedron satisfying \(P\subseteq Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in Q}c^\top x\le\min_{x\in P}c^\top x=\min_{x\in X}c^\top x\), with possible strict inequality when \(Q\supsetneq P\).

notation.meaning: convex hull of feasible Boolean points

children.title: Cutting-Plane Optimization Boundary
children.top_down_role: General cutting-plane development beyond PB reasoning and certification needs.

knowledge_statements.title: Cutting-Plane Optimization Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States when valid-inequality refinement supplies bounds and when it constitutes an exact optimization method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^n\) be a nonempty feasible set, let \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(Q_0\supseteq\operatorname{conv}(X)\) be a polyhedral relaxation. Suppose the relevant minima over \(X\) and the relaxations are finite and attained. A cutting-plane step selects an inequality \(a^\top x\le b\) that is valid for every \(x\in X\) and violated by a current relaxation minimizer, then sets \(Q_{k+1}=Q_k\cap\{x:a^\top x\le b\}\). Every minimization value over \(Q_k\) is a valid lower bound. Exactness requires eventual production of an optimal integral point together with a matching bound; validity of individual cuts alone does not ensure finite termination or closure of the integrality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Valid cuts preserve all feasible integer points and strengthen valid lower bounds, but exact optimization additionally requires an optimal integral point and a matching bound; cut validity alone does not guarantee finite termination.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^n\) is nonempty, \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(Q_0\supseteq\operatorname{conv}(X)\).
The relevant minima over \(X\) and \(Q_k\) are finite and attained.
Each generated inequality is valid for \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{k+1}\supseteq\operatorname{conv}(X)\) and \(\min_{x\in Q_k}c^\top x\le\min_{x\in X}c^\top x\); validity alone does not imply finite exactness.

children.title: Branching Framework Boundary
children.top_down_role: General branch-based optimization frameworks outside MaxSAT or PB-specific search.

knowledge_statements.title: Branching Framework Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes exactness of finite branching independently of node-selection and bound-strengthening policies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) be finite. At a search node representing \(X_N\subseteq X\), a valid branching disjunction consists of children \(X_{N,1},\ldots,X_{N,r}\) satisfying \(X_N=\bigcup_{j=1}^r X_{N,j}\). A branch-and-bound framework is exact if every unpruned branch is eventually resolved and a node is pruned only because it is infeasible or because a valid lower bound is no better than the incumbent value. Branching without exhaustive resolution or sound pruning remains a search heuristic and cannot certify global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branching certifies an optimum only when children cover the parent, pruning is sound, and every potentially improving branch is eventually resolved.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite.
Each branching disjunction covers its parent feasible set.
Every pruning bound is valid for its node.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Upon exhaustive sound termination, the incumbent \(x^\star\) satisfies \(f(x^\star)=\min_{x\in X}f(x)\).

notation.meaning: feasible assignments represented by node N

review_flags: No supplied source locator specifically covers branch-and-bound coverage, pruning, and termination conditions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coverage, sound-pruning, and exhaustive-resolution boundary is plausible, but no locator supports it, and the objective f should be explicitly introduced as a function on X.

children.title: Decomposition Framework Boundary
children.top_down_role: General decomposition architectures beyond directly relevant Boolean optimization interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Framework Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies structural separability as a sufficient condition for independent block optimization and valid coordination as the general requirement for linked decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{f(x):x\in X\}\) with variables partitioned as \(x=(x^1,\ldots,x^p)\). If the feasible set and objective separate as \(X=X_1\times\cdots\times X_p\) and \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^p f_i(x^i)\), independent exact optimization of the blocks is exact for the global problem. When linking constraints or shared variables destroy this product structure, independently optimal block solutions need not be mutually compatible. An exact decomposition method must then use coordination, such as a valid master problem, prices, or cuts, sufficient to establish global feasibility and optimality; isolated subproblem solutions alone provide no general global certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full separability makes independent block optimization exact. With linking structure, isolated block optima need not be compatible, so an exact decomposition generally requires valid coordination and a global certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is nonempty and the displayed minima are attained.
The variable blocks form a fixed partition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(X=\prod_{i=1}^pX_i\) and \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^pf_i(x^i)\), then \(\min_{x\in X}f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^p\min_{u\in X_i}f_i(u)\); without this separability, the equality need not hold.

children.title: Boolean Optimization Interface

knowledge_statements.title: Boolean Optimization Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the exact interface between Boolean models and finite zero-one mathematical programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) be Boolean variables and identify truth assignments with vectors \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) by \(x_i=1\) exactly when \(v_i\) is true. For a Boolean constraint formula \(F\), define \(X_F=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:x\models F\}\). Any objective \(f\) on assignments then yields the equivalent finite program \(\min\{f(x):x\in X_F\}\). Conversely, any zero-one feasible set specified by constraints defines a Boolean relation on the corresponding variables. The interface preserves feasibility and objective values only when auxiliary variables are existentially projected and any encoding constraints are logically exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Truth assignments correspond to zero-one vectors, so Boolean constraints and objectives form a finite zero-one program when the encoding and auxiliary-variable projection are exact.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) contains finitely many Boolean variables.
Any auxiliary encoding variables are existentially quantified when projected to the original variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\{f(\alpha):\alpha\models F\}=\min\{f(x):x\in X_F\}\) under the truth-to-one identification.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly documents the Boolean-to-zero-one representation and projection convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role and truth-to-zero-one correspondence fit the leaf, but no locator supports the bidirectional encoding and existential-projection conditions.

children.title: Quadratic Boolean Optimization Boundary
children.top_down_role: Quadratic objective structures outside native linear PB formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Boolean Optimization Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixes degree two as the native limit of quadratic unconstrained Boolean optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A quadratic unconstrained Boolean optimization instance has the form \(\min\{c+\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i+\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}q_{ij}x_ix_j:x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\). Because \(x_i^2=x_i\) on the Boolean domain, every polynomial of degree at most two has this form after collecting terms. A polynomial containing a nonzero square-free monomial \(\prod_{i\in S}x_i\) with \(|S|\ge3\) lies outside the native quadratic representation unless auxiliary variables, penalties, or additional constraints are introduced. Such a reformulation must preserve projected feasible objective values to remain exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: QUBO natively represents Boolean polynomials of degree at most two; genuine higher-degree monomials require an exact auxiliary-variable or constrained reformulation.
assumptions_latex: Polynomial terms are reduced using \(x_i^k=x_i\) for every integer \(k\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The native model contains exactly reduced Boolean polynomials of degree at most \(2\); a nonzero monomial on at least three distinct variables requires reformulation.

children.title: Higher-Order Boolean Optimization Boundary
children.top_down_role: Boolean objectives containing interactions beyond quadratic order.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Boolean Optimization Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates genuine multilinear degree above two from native quadratic Boolean models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) has a unique multilinear polynomial representation \(f(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}}c_S\prod_{i\in S}x_i\). Its Boolean degree is \(\max\{|S|:c_S\ne0\}\), with the zero function assigned degree \(-\infty\). Higher-order Boolean optimization comprises instances whose reduced objective or constraints contain a term of degree at least three. Such terms cannot be retained verbatim in a quadratic model; quadratization is a distinct representation step whose auxiliary-variable projection and objective correspondence must be checked.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Boolean model is genuinely higher-order when its unique multilinear representation has a nonzero term involving at least three distinct variables.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a real-valued function on \(\{0,1\}^n\).
Polynomial expressions are reduced to multilinear form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is higher-order exactly when \(\max\{|S|:c_S\ne0\}\ge3\).

children.title: Linearization Interface
children.top_down_role: Reformulation links that bring nonlinear Boolean objectives into linear optimization models.

knowledge_statements.title: Linearization Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the exact linear extended formulation for one binary bilinear product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For binary variables \(x_i,x_j\in\{0,1\}\), introduce \(y_{ij}\) and impose \(y_{ij}\le x_i\), \(y_{ij}\le x_j\), \(y_{ij}\ge x_i+x_j-1\), and \(y_{ij}\ge0\). These inequalities force \(y_{ij}=x_ix_j\) at every binary pair. Therefore replacing each occurrence of \(x_ix_j\) by \(y_{ij}\), together with these constraints, preserves the feasible values and objective values after projection onto the original variables. If the original variables are relaxed to \([0,1]\), the same inequalities describe the convex hull of the bilinear graph over binary endpoints, not equality with the nonlinear product at every fractional point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Four linear inequalities exactly encode a product of two binary variables; under continuous relaxation they give the convex hull, not pointwise bilinear equality.
assumptions_latex: \(y_{ij}\) replaces every modeled occurrence of \(x_ix_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_{ij}=x_ix_j\) if and only if \(0\le y_{ij}\), \(y_{ij}\le x_i\), \(y_{ij}\le x_j\), and \(y_{ij}\ge x_i+x_j-1\).

children.title: Auxiliary-Variable Expansion
children.top_down_role: Model-size and semantic effects of representing nonlinear interactions with auxiliary variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Variable Expansion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Provides an exact recursive expansion of a higher-order binary monomial into quadratic relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a monomial \(m(x)=\prod_{k=1}^d x_{i_k}\) with distinct binary variables and \(d\ge3\), introduce binary variables \(y_2,\ldots,y_d\). Enforce \(y_2=x_{i_1}x_{i_2}\) and \(y_k=y_{k-1}x_{i_k}\) for \(k\in\{3,\ldots,d\}\), encoding every product relation by the exact binary linearization inequalities. Then \(y_k=\prod_{r=1}^k x_{i_r}\) for every feasible extended assignment, so \(y_d=m(x)\). Projection onto \(x\) admits every original Boolean assignment and assigns it a unique chain of product values; hence substituting \(y_d\) for the monomial is exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degree-d binary monomial can be represented exactly by a chain of d−1 binary product variables and exact pairwise linearizations.
assumptions_latex: Every recursive product relation is imposed by an exact binary linearization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_d=\prod_{k=1}^d x_{i_k}\), and projection of the extended formulation onto \(x\) is \(\{0,1\}^n\).
